To determine the probability that heads never occur on consecutive tosses in 10 flips of a fair coin, we use a recursive approach. Let \( S(n) \) denote the number of valid sequences of length \( n \) with no two consecutive heads. The recurrence relation for \( S(n) \) is:

\[
S(n) = S(n-1) + S(n-2)
\]

with base cases \( S(1) = 2 \) and \( S(2) = 3 \). This recurrence relation is the same as the Fibonacci sequence shifted by two positions, i.e., \( S(n) = \text{Fib}(n+2) \).

Calculating the Fibonacci numbers up to \( \text{Fib}(12) \):

\[
\begin{align*}
\text{Fib}(1) & = 1, \\
\text{Fib}(2) & = 1, \\
\text{Fib}(3) & = 2, \\
\text{Fib}(4) & = 3, \\
\text{Fib}(5) & = 5, \\
\text{Fib}(6) & = 8, \\
\text{Fib}(7) & = 13, \\
\text{Fib}(8) & = 21, \\
\text{Fib}(9) & = 34, \\
\text{Fib}(10) & = 55, \\
\text{Fib}(11) & = 89, \\
\text{Fib}(12) & = 144.
\end{align*}
\]

Thus, \( S(10) = \text{Fib}(12) = 144 \).

The total number of possible outcomes when flipping a coin 10 times is \( 2^{10} = 1024 \). The probability is therefore:

\[
\frac{144}{1024} = \frac{9}{64}
\]

Reducing the fraction to lowest terms, we get \( \frac{9}{64} \). Hence, \( i = 9 \) and \( j = 64 \), leading to \( i + j = 9 + 64 = 73 \).

\[
\boxed{73}
\]
